items.title: A New Vision for Human Work After Automation
items.content: Hey, welcome back to the Every Podcast, where we talk about the future of work. I'm Natalia Quintero, and at Every, our team of writers and builders use AI every day, so we can tell you how the frontier is shifting, what actually works, and what you need to know. So last week at Every, we hosted our first ever conference, V.C.S.S., It was a full day of talks in Brooklyn featuring speakers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Notion, Lovable, Ode, and many more. If you missed it, we'll have all of the talks available at every.to forward slash TV. We built the whole day around one question. What does great human work look like after automation? Dan Shipper, Every's co-founder and CEO, closed the conference with his answer, which you'll hear later in this episode. He took our quarterly customer survey results and built a custom CRM, then a video game, and then personally reached out to a pretty vast number of our customers. In pre-AI terms, he did the work of about five people, a data scientist, a game developer, a marketer, an engineer, and a salesperson. But instead, he did all of that work with a single clot subscription over the course of a single week. And if you ask Claude what it sees in the same survey, you'll probably get a generic answer that anyone could get. And that's actually Dan's point. Great work is the perspective you bring to the model. So for the podcast this week, Dan's closing talk from our conference thesis. Enjoy. Thesis, did everyone have a good time? Woo! Well, we gathered here to answer one question, which is what is the future of great human work after automation? I hope you got some good answers today. Did you get some good answers? Yes? Yes? All right. I wanna add my take. Hopefully I can help bring it together a little bit. So I really, I love this question. And obviously, because we built the conference around it, it's really the question that we try to answer every day at every, And what's really interesting about this question is you're really trying to predict the future. And there's two, I think, real methods for predicting the future. One is what I'll call the aggregate, where you gather lots and lots of data, and then you extrapolate a trend line. And the other is called the intimate, where you zoom in on one real case or real situation, and then you extrapolate from there. And in our culture, we tend to emphasize the aggregate. The aggregate is objective, it's quantitative, and the intimate kind of feels a little bit anecdotal. And the aggregate's also extremely powerful. The reason we have AI is the aggregate, is for example, scaling loss. We found that if you put more data and compute on one end of the system, you get more capability out. And all of us here are here because we're riding that curve that you can see in the aggregate. We also use the aggregate to answer this question that we have come here for. What does work look like after automation? A good example is GDP Val from OpenAI. It's a benchmark which measures how good models are at doing economically valuable tasks. And the way it works is they have a bunch of experts pick tasks from their job, real tasks, and they turn it into a prompt. They give the prompts to a model, and they give a prompt to a human that's not using AI, and then blind experts pick which one is better, the human version or the AI version. And the prompts are very, very detailed. They look something like this. And in 2024, with GPT-4-0, experts, or AI, won against a human expert 12.4% of the time. In 2025 it was 47.6 and in 2026 it was about 83%. This is with GPT 5.4, I'm sure it's higher now. I'm sure this benchmark is saturated. You look at that, an AI is beating a human 83% of the time according to blind human experts at expert work. And I can also see this in my work, in the way that I work. If we look at my week, last week. We ran our quarterly customer survey. And in the cracks of my calendar, in the middle of all of the things that I had going on, I analyzed the s…

items.title: Why the Cyberpocalypse Might Hit China Harder
items.content: Chang Che is a writer and contributor to the New Yorker . In August, researchers at a California security firm used an OpenAI model to find a software bug in PHP, a programming language that undergird some seventy per cent of the world’s websites, including Wikipedia and WordPress. They alerted PHP’s developers, who quietly began working on a fix. By late October, the fix was ready, but before they could alert the world, the break-in attempts had begun. Days earlier, Amazon detected someone trying to hack into its servers; attacks code began circulating online. Some governments and companies began pulling websites down, rather than risk a security breach. One security firm described the flaws as some of the worst ever found in PHP, “and arguably in software history.” Before AI, the internet might have looked, to a hacker, like a worn-out bug screen. You could discern some holes with a keen eye, and that knowledge was reliably asymmetric—others probably didn’t know about the holes you found. Moreover, tunneling through the holes undetected took months or years of human labor, talent, and money. Now, with AI, the internet looks more like a block of Swiss cheese: the holes are obvious, anyone can, or will, see them, and the time and cost it takes to exploit these software flaws have plunged alarmingly fast . According to Google’s incident response team , the average time it takes for cyber criminals to exploit a new vulnerability is -7 days, meaning hacking attempts are “routinely occurring before a patch is even released.” A China Central Television (CCTV) feature about the PHP vulnerability discovered by cybersecurity firm Calif, with the aid of OpenAI models. Source . Hackers refer to unbeknownst software bugs like PHP as “zero-days” because a defender has had zero days to protect themselves upon its discovery. Once a hacker discovers a zero-day in, say, iOS software, every iPhone user is potentially…

items.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. items.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. items.title: Ep 96: Nebius CTO on Racing the Hyperscalers Before AWS Wakes Up
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:15 If NVIDIA could have bought... Like, could have produced, like, 10 x the chips, this whole market would have been shaped differently. Yeah. Because there is not enough capacity for their scale, this is a relatively small business for them. For the hyperscalers, it's not just a matter of, like, sales. Speaker 1 | 00:15 - 00:29 It's also a matter of changing the infrastructure that was built at scale for other kinds of workloads. This is a massive investment on their part that needs to be justified by the size of a potential business, and it's not that there yet. Speaker 2 | 00:33 - 01:08 The emergence of Nebius and the other hyperscaler competitors these past years has been a fascinating part of the AI story. It's something I've really been interested in, and so it was a lot of fun to have Nebius' CTO, Neela, on the podcast because we're able to dig into a bunch of interesting things about the business and how the space has unfolded. We talked about Nebius' really interesting origin story and the original relationship with Yandex and how the company came to be. We talked about what it's like to be inside one of these companies, how Nebius works, you know, with NVIDIA, what it looks like to get their next generation of chips live. We talked about why the opportunity actually existed and why AWS, GCP, Azure, didn't just capture this entire market. items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI
items.content: In the AI race thus far, openness has been China’s secret sauce. As fast followers to the frontier, Chinese AI companies have gained trust by publicizing their weights and architectures. And at the cost of revenue, they have achieved global adoption, brand recognition, and a truly competitive dynamic with American labs. Last week, China’s Ministries of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Science and Technology (MOST) jointly proposed expanding China’s catalogue of export-controlled technologies, with most of the proposed regulations taking aim at subsets of China’s AI industry. Regulators will spend a month taking comments on the draft before anything becomes law, but we can already learn a ton from this announcement in its current form. Does Beijing want to hold back the tides of open models? Why is MOFCOM writing these rules now, and what does this say about the Chinese government’s appetite for AI-enabled risks versus growth? To find out, we spent three days poring over the draft regulations — so you don’t have to! What’s ahead: How these rules came to be — and how this draft is already affecting the Chinese AI industry; What the proposed rules mean for frontier models, chip design, memory, cybersecurity, AI content detection, and even China’s minority languages; Who actually decides which export licenses get approved, and the balance of power between provincial and central authorities; What these rules tell us about Beijing’s expectations for AI development. The 40 proposed additions in Announcement 48, split across AI, photovoltaics, and biomedicine. Today, we’re just focusing on the AI-related regulations, but a future piece tackling everything else — from this announcement’s proposed restrictions on PV cells and gene therapies, to other recent announcements on port dredgers and tunnel borers — is in the works!
